From the git histories of four bodies of law · 1949 to 2026

Law in motion

We hold every amendment to the German Basic Law since 1949, eight years of changes to nine US Code titles, the Swiss constitution with its data-protection and debt-collection acts, and the UK's special-educational-needs law. Each change is a dated commit. Read together, they show how law grows, how narrowly it changes, and how often it quietly switches itself off again.

Across sixteen jurisdictions · updated every half hour

Analyses from the research agenda, rerun on everything loaded so far: Germany, Switzerland, the UK, the US, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Gibraltar, Hong Kong, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Malta, Monaco, Slovakia and Slovenia. Each round adds the repositories that gained history since the last one.

Everything here is computed from the commit metadata and file history of lexifina/grundgesetz, swiss-law, uk-law-history and us-code-history as checked out on 28 October 2026, with no model in the loop. The US Code history begins with the 2017 edition and the Swiss history with 2019, so earlier changes there are not shown. The other repositories were still being built during the run, so later rebuilds may shift a figure slightly.

Literature review · 28 Oct 2026

What to do with a holistic dataset of law

Thirteen lines of research that measure or picture legal change, what each one did, and what we could do better. Most published work studies one country, one level or one snapshot. Our dataset has every provision, in every jurisdiction, at every in-force date, with the law that changed it. That makes several long-standing questions answerable for the first time. Four of them are already run on the Findings tab: wording survival, readability of amendments, the temporary-law detector and constitutional growth.

Read the papers before quoting their numbers.

    "Runnable now" means the four histories we hold (German Basic Law 1949–2017, Swiss BV, DSG and SchKG since 2019, UK SEND law 2014–2021, nine US Code titles since 2017) are enough for a first version. "Needs more" means the result only means something once more jurisdictions or bodies of law are loaded.
